newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-TRAINER SAYS MCCALL'S AS CLEAN AS A CHITLIN.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-TRAINER SAYS MCCALL'S AS CLEAN AS A CHITLIN.

text.p: For the record, Oliver McCall is as clean as a chitlin.

That was the word on Wednesday from his trainer George Benton when asked if McCall, who receives daily counselling as part of his drug rehabilitation programme, will be drug-free for his Friday night fight with Lennox Lewis for the World Boxing Council heavyweight title.
For the uninitiated, that's chitlin as in chitlins or chitterlings or pigs' intestines, a popular holiday dish in the American South. Chitlins must be thoroughly washed to be served safely.

In addition to his counselling, McCall, who in recent years has alternated visits to drug programmes with trips to police stations, has found religion to help him overcome an addiction he said dates to when he was 13 years old.

McCall's latest run-in with the law was last December when he was arrested for resisting arrest after allegedly throwing an ashtray and a glass in a hotel bar in Nashville, Tennessee, and throwing a Christmas tree in the hotel lobby.
But through the help of constant counselling and his newfound religion, McCall insists he will stay clean in his latest rehabilitation programme.

"When I actually seen the light, it was revealed to me that Jesus Christ was my Lord and Saviour," McCall said on Wednesday. "Whoever wins the fight, all the glory goes to God. This is a wicked and cruel world and praise the Lord."

The 31-year-old McCall said he had gone to a support meeting for people battling drug addiction as recently as the previous night. He paid tribute to his counsellor, whom he talks to every day, and acknowledged that "I will be in treatment the rest of my life."
"He has guys (drug counsellors) that follow him around. He's gotta be clean," Benton said. "He's as clean as a chitlin."

Nevada State Athletic Commission Executive Director Marc Ratner said Wednesday the commission put McCall, who like Lewis is 31, through a "complete battery of tests, including a drug test, which we don't normally do until after the fight.
"But this is a special situation because of his history. I'm completely confident he'll be clean. This fight is very important to him. He's not a dumb man."
But the betting is 5-1 against McCall beating Lewis for the second time to win the vacant WBC title.

McCall beat Lewis in September 1994 to win the WBC title and then lost it to Briton Frank Bruno, who lost it to Mike Tyson last March. The WBC belt was not on the line when Evander Holyfield beat Tyson last November.
Emanuel Steward trained McCall when he upset Lewis, stopping him with one punch in the second round after Lewis missed with a right hand, leaving his chin exposed like a rank amateur.

But Steward switched camps for this fight and Lewis (29-1) says he has learned a lot from Steward, who seems to have improved his fighter's balance and taught him that it is not against the law to throw a jab with some power.
McCall (28-6) said: "I would prefer Emanuel Steward to be in his corner. I know exactly what Emanuel Steward is teaching him to use against me.

"He's going to try to put the punches together real tight (short, not looping), and when he puts them together real tight there's going to be an atomic explosion," said McCall, playing off his ring name "Atomic Bull."

Referring to Lewis's reputation as a reluctant warrior -- at least before his last fight, a narrow victory over Ray Mercer last May -- McCall said recently that "they can tell him how to fight, but they can't put the fight into him.
